notes.b: Brazil is an agricultural superpower. Its farms feed the world market far more than they employ its own people, which shows how mechanised and commercial the leading sector is.
points: Brazil is the world's largest producer and exporter of soya beans, and the largest producer and exporter of coffee, which is about a third of world output (2020s).
It is also the largest producer of sugar cane and orange juice, and the largest exporter of beef and chicken, so it leads the world in several different foods.
Agriculture itself is under a tenth of GDP and of jobs (early 2020s). This is small because a few huge, machine-run farms produce the crops with few workers.
Agribusiness as a whole (farming plus processing and trade) is much larger than farming alone, and it makes up a large share of Brazil's exports.
notes.tip: Use the contrast between a world-leading output and a small share of GDP and jobs to show that Brazilian farming is highly mechanised.

notes.b: Brazilian farming ranges from giant mechanised farms to tiny family plots. Exams ask for two types, so learn each with a crop and a place.
points: Large commercial mechanised farms grow soya, maize and cotton in the Cerrado (the tropical savanna of the Centre-West). Machines suit the flat land, so a few workers farm huge areas.
Plantations grow one crop on a large estate for sale abroad, such as sugar cane, coffee and oranges.
Extensive cattle ranching uses large areas of land with few animals per hectare and little labour, on the Cerrado, the Pantanal and cleared Amazon land.

Subsistence and family farming grows food for the household and local sale: cassava (manioc), beans and maize. It includes shifting cultivation in the Amazon and small farms in the sertão (the dry Northeast interior).
Irrigated fruit farming uses river water to grow export fruit in the dry Northeast, for example grapes and mangoes.
notes.tip: If asked for two types, name the type, one crop and one region for each, for example mechanised soya in the Cerrado and family farms in the sertão.

notes.b: The Cerrado has a rainy summer and a dry winter, and farmers have fitted two crops into the rains. This doubles what each field yields in a year.
points: Soya is planted with the first rains, about October, because the seeds need moist soil to germinate.
The soya is harvested about January to February, which clears the field while the rains are still falling.
A second crop of maize, called the safrinha (Portuguese for 'little harvest'), is then planted in the same rainy season, so the same land gives two crops a year.
The dry winter, about May to September, is the harvest and rest period. The calendar works only because the rain is reliable in summer.

notes.h: Coffee: boom, frost and move north
notes.b: Coffee made 19th-century São Paulo rich, but frost pushed the crop north. Its history links climate, soil, labour and ports.
points: The coffee boom in São Paulo state in the 19th century was worked first by enslaved Africans and then by European immigrants, and the beans were exported through the port of Santos.
The 'black frost' of July 1975 destroyed most coffee trees in Paraná, because coffee bushes die in hard frost. The risk of frost shaped where coffee is now grown.
Minas Gerais is now the leading coffee state, and Brazil remains the world's largest coffee producer, with about a third of world output.
notes.tip: Link coffee to terra roxa (the soil from basalt that suited it), and to frost in the south, to show physical factors at work.

notes.b: Within a few decades Brazil turned acidic, infertile savanna into the world's biggest soya belt. Science, flat land and cheap land made it possible.
points: Cerrado soils are acidic and high in aluminium, so for a long time they were thought useless for crops. Adding crushed limestone (liming) and fertiliser made them productive.
EMBRAPA, the state agricultural research body founded in 1973, bred tropical soya varieties that grow well in the heat and day length of the Cerrado.
The land is cheap and flat, which suits large machines, and the summer rain is reliable, so two crops a year are possible.
Mato Grosso is Brazil's leading soya state, and China buys most of Brazil's soya exports (2020s), which gives farmers a huge market.
notes.tip: Examiners ask about technology such as EMBRAPA's work. Give the problem (acid soil), the solution (liming, new varieties) and the result (Mato Grosso soya).

notes.b: Sugar was Brazil's first great export crop and is now also a fuel. The story shows how a colonial crop became a modern energy industry.
points: Colonial sugar plantations grew on the dark, fertile massapê soils of the Northeast coast, using enslaved labour.
Today São Paulo state is the leading sugar-cane state, and Brazil is the world's largest producer of sugar cane.
Proálcool (the National Alcohol Programme, 1975) was launched after the oil crisis so that Brazil could make fuel from cane instead of importing oil.
Flex-fuel cars, sold from 2003, run on ethanol, petrol or any mix, so drivers can choose whichever is cheaper.

notes.b: Brazil has more cattle than people, and ranching is one of its biggest land uses. It brings export income but also forest loss.
points: Brazil has one of the world's largest cattle herds, with more cattle than people (2020s), and it is the largest exporter of beef.
Extensive ranching takes place on the Cerrado, in the Pantanal wetland and on cleared Amazon land, because cattle need large areas of cheap grass.
Cattle ranching is the largest single cause of Amazon clearance, as ranchers burn forest to make pasture.
Gaúchos (cattle herders) work the grasslands of the Pampa in Rio Grande do Sul in the far south.
notes.tip: Keep deforestation to one sentence here: ranching is the largest single cause of Amazon clearance.

notes.h: Irrigated fruit in the São Francisco valley
notes.b: In a dry region, a river can turn desert-like land into export farmland. The São Francisco does this for the Northeast.
points: Petrolina (Pernambuco) and Juazeiro (Bahia) face each other across the São Francisco River and export grapes and mangoes.
Water comes from the river and its dams, such as Sobradinho, whose lake is one of the world's largest artificial lakes by area.
Irrigation turns the semi-arid sertão, where rain is low and unreliable, into reliable farmland, and the sunny climate suits fruit.
Where irrigation water evaporates it can leave salt in the soil (salinisation), which is a risk for these farms.

notes.b: Brazil's land, climate and rivers give it natural advantages that few countries can match.
points: A huge area of flat land makes it easy to use big machines and to expand farms.
Tropical temperatures allow two or three crops a year, because there is no cold season to stop growth in most regions.
Heavy rainfall over most of the country supplies crops without irrigation.
Fertile soils, such as terra roxa on the Paraná Plateau basalt and massapê on the Northeast coast, give high yields for coffee and sugar.
Rivers provide water for irrigation, for example the São Francisco in the Northeast.
notes.tip: Terra roxa comes from basalt, not from the Amazon. Do not call Amazon soils fertile, except várzea and terra preta.

notes.b: Climate and soil also hold farming back in many areas. Each problem has a cause in the physical geography.
points: Latosols (the red-yellow Amazon and Cerrado soils) are leached by heat and rain and are acidic and low in nutrients, so crops fail without lime and fertiliser.
Drought in the sertão (rain about 250 to 800 mm a year, varying greatly) makes farming unreliable and drives people away.
Frost in the south destroys crops such as coffee, as in July 1975.
Erosion after clearance strips thin soil once trees no longer hold it, and pests and diseases thrive in the warm, humid tropics.

notes.h: Human and economic factors: who owns the land
notes.b: Land ownership shapes who farms and who gains. Brazil's is among the most unequal in the world.
points: A latifúndio is a very large estate; a minifúndio is a tiny plot. Huge estates sit beside tiny plots, so most farmland is held by few owners.
Landless rural workers press for land, and the MST (Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra, founded 1984) is their movement, not a government body.
Family farms grow most of the food eaten at home, while big agribusiness exports, so the biggest earners are not the main food growers.
Credit and technology favour large farms, so small farmers struggle to buy machines and inputs.
High transport costs to the ports cut profits, especially for farms far inland.
notes.tip: The MST is a movement, not a government body, and Bolsa Família is a cash-transfer scheme, not land reform.

notes.h: Markets and government policy in farming
notes.b: Where crops can be sold, and what the state does, decide what farmers grow.
points: Export markets such as China and the EU buy soya, beef and coffee and set demand and prices.
Mercosur (founded 1991 by the Treaty of Asunción: Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay) gives Brazilian farm goods a regional market.
EMBRAPA research improves seeds, soils and methods, so yields keep rising.
The Amazon soy moratorium (2006) is an agreement by traders not to buy soya grown on newly cleared Amazon land.
Farm credit for family farms helps small producers buy seed and equipment.
notes.tip: Examiners list markets, technology, land ownership and government policy among the factors influencing agriculture. Pick factors and give a named example for each.

notes.b: Brazil's farming success has costs, from violence to dependence on world prices.
points: Land conflict and violence are common on the Amazon frontier, where ranchers, farmers and settlers fight over land.
Deforestation for pasture and soya clears forest, which brings international criticism.
Heavy pesticide use pollutes land and water and affects the health of workers.
Dependence on world commodity prices means that when the price of soya or coffee falls, farm incomes and export earnings fall too.

notes.b: The Amazon forest gives timber and other products. Some are taken sustainably and some are not.
points: Amazon timber is heavily logged, much of it illegally. Mahogany was one of the most heavily logged species.
Brazil nuts are collected from wild trees and rubber is tapped from standing forest, so these products can be harvested without clearing it.
The rubber boom, about 1879 to 1912, was centred on Manaus and built its wealth, for example the Teatro Amazonas opera house (1896).
The boom collapsed because Henry Wickham took rubber seeds from the Amazon to Britain in 1876, and plantations in British Asia (Malaya) later undercut wild Amazon rubber on price.

notes.b: Extractive reserves let local people earn a living from the forest while keeping it standing.
points: Chico Mendes was a rubber tapper and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest and the people who tapped it.
He was murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988, which brought world attention to the fight over the Amazon.
The Chico Mendes Extractive Reserve in Acre was created in 1990. In reserves like it, local people harvest forest products, such as rubber and nuts, without clearing the forest.

notes.b: Fast-growing plantations meet industrial demand, and satellite figures show how fast natural forest has been lost.
points: Eucalyptus plantations in the Southeast and South supply pulp and paper, because eucalyptus grows fast in the warm, wet climate.
Brazil is the world's largest exporter of pulp (2020s).
PRODES (the satellite measure of Amazon clearance) recorded about 27,800 km² cleared in 2004, about 4,600 km² in 2012 and about 13,000 km² in 2021.
About a fifth of the Brazilian Amazon's original forest has been cleared.
The Forest Code says Amazon landholders must keep 80% of their land under forest, and the Amazon Fund (2008), paid for mainly by Norway and also Germany, finances protection.
notes.tip: Use the PRODES figures to show a fall from 2004 to 2012 and a rise by 2021. There is more on this in the Geoecology notes on the felling of the Amazon.

notes.b: Brazil has a very long coast but a small fishing industry, and the reason is in the ocean.
points: The warm Brazil Current flows south along the coast and is low in plankton, so there is little food for fish and fishing is small for so long a coastline (about 7,400 km).
Artisanal (small-boat) fishing is the main sea fishing on the Northeast coast.
Amazon river fisheries catch pirarucu (arapaima, one of the largest freshwater fish) and tambaqui.
Aquaculture is growing: tilapia is the main farmed fish, and shrimp farms are found in Ceará and Rio Grande do Norte in the Northeast.

notes.b: Brazil has huge mineral wealth, especially iron ore, and the mines shape regions.
points: Carajás in Pará, discovered in 1967 and run by Vale, is the world's largest iron-ore mine. The ore travels about 890 km by the Carajás Railway to the port of São Luís in Maranhão.
The Iron Quadrangle (Quadrilátero Ferrífero) in Minas Gerais is another iron-ore region, and the 18th-century gold rush happened around Ouro Preto.
Bauxite (the ore of aluminium) is mined at Trombetas in Pará.
Brazil produces most of the world's niobium, used in steel alloys, at Araxá in Minas Gerais.

notes.b: Mining brings export income, but accidents and illegal mines cause deaths and lasting pollution.
points: A tailings dam stores the waste mud from a mine. At Mariana, Minas Gerais, on 5 November 2015 the Fundão dam (Samarco, owned by Vale and BHP) collapsed, killing 19 people, and mud polluted the Rio Doce all the way to the Atlantic.
At Brumadinho, Minas Gerais, on 25 January 2019 a Vale tailings dam collapsed, with about 270 deaths.
Illegal gold miners (garimpeiros) in Yanomami territory in Roraima pollute rivers with mercury, which poisons fish and people.
A health emergency was declared among the Yanomami in 2023 because of illegal mining.
notes.tip: Give the date, the place, the owner and the deaths for each dam disaster to turn a general point about mining costs into named examples.

notes.b: Brazil's rain-fed rivers give it one of the cleanest electricity supplies of any large economy.
points: Hydroelectricity supplies about three-fifths of Brazil's electricity, because heavy rain on the plateau feeds fast-flowing rivers.
Renewables (hydro, wind, solar and biomass) give about 85 to 90% of electricity (early 2020s), so Brazil's electricity is among the cleanest of large economies.
Wind farms in Bahia and Rio Grande do Norte, and solar, are growing fast in the Northeast, where winds and sun are strong.

notes.b: From a state-owned company to deep-sea discoveries, oil has made Brazil a major producer.
points: Petrobras was founded in 1953 under the slogan 'the oil is ours', as a state company to control Brazil's oil.
The Campos Basin, off Rio de Janeiro state, has been producing from the 1970s.

Pre-salt fields in the Santos Basin were discovered in 2006 to 2007. They lie up to about 300 km offshore, several kilometres below the sea surface and under a thick layer of salt, so drilling is hard and costly.
The pre-salt fields now supply most of Brazil's oil, and Brazil is one of the world's ten largest oil producers (2020s).

notes.b: Brazil also gets energy from crops and a little from uranium.
points: Ethanol from sugar cane is a transport fuel, used in flex-fuel cars, which cuts Brazil's need for imported oil.
Angra dos Reis, in Rio de Janeiro state, has Brazil's nuclear power station, a small share of its supply.

notes.b: Brazil's early economy sent raw goods abroad, so manufacturing started late.
points: Brazilwood, sugar, gold, rubber and coffee were exported raw, so little manufacturing developed before 1900.
Coffee profits later financed São Paulo's first factories, which is why São Paulo became the industrial centre.

notes.b: From the 1930s the state decided to build industry behind tariff walls rather than import factory goods.
points: Import substitution industrialisation (ISI) means making goods at home that were once imported, protecting the new factories with tariffs.
Under Getúlio Vargas (in power 1930 to 1945 and 1951 to 1954) the state built heavy industry: the CSN steelworks at Volta Redonda began production in 1946, and Petrobras was founded in 1953.

Under Juscelino Kubitschek (president 1956 to 1961), whose slogan was 'fifty years of progress in five', foreign car makers were invited into the ABC region (Santo André, São Bernardo do Campo and São Caetano do Sul) near São Paulo. Volkswagen's São Bernardo plant opened in 1959.

notes.h: The military period and the Brazilian miracle
notes.b: Rule by the generals mixed fast growth with huge state projects and then a debt crisis.
points: Military rule lasted from 1964 to 1985, and the 'Brazilian miracle', about 1968 to 1973, was a period of very fast growth.
State projects included Itaipu, Carajás and the Trans-Amazonian Highway (begun 1970, opened 1972).
Embraer was founded in 1969 at São José dos Campos and is now the world's third-largest maker of commercial jets.
The 1980s brought a debt crisis and hyperinflation (prices rising very fast).

notes.b: From the 1990s Brazil ended hyperinflation and opened its economy.
points: The Real Plan (1994) ended hyperinflation, which gave firms stable prices for investing.
Privatisation sold state firms: Embraer in 1994 and Vale in 1997.
Mercosur (1991) opened a regional market for Brazilian manufactured goods.

notes.h: Raw materials as a location factor
notes.b: Industry grows where its inputs are, and Brazil has many raw materials near its industry. This is one of the factors examiners ask for.
points: Iron ore from Minas Gerais and Carajás feeds the steel industry, for example the CSN works at Volta Redonda.
Sugar cane is turned into ethanol.
Soya and meat supply food processing, and JBS is the world's largest meat-processing company.
Eucalyptus supplies the pulp and paper industry.
Oil supplies petrochemicals, so oil fields lead to refining and chemical plants.
notes.tip: If asked for two factors, raw materials is a safe choice. Name the material, the industry it feeds and the place.

notes.b: Factories need power, and cheap hydroelectricity has pulled industry to certain places.
points: Itaipu, on the Paraná and shared with Paraguay, supplies the Southeast industrial core with cheap hydroelectricity.
Tucuruí Dam on the Tocantins in Pará (1984) powers aluminium smelting in the Amazon, a very energy-hungry industry.
Rain on the plateau feeds the rivers, so cheap power is available at low cost to industry.
notes.tip: Itaipu is shared with Paraguay. Say so when you name it.

notes.b: Industry needs workers, and Brazil's population has supplied both cheap labour and skills.
points: A large, low-cost workforce keeps wages low for factories, which attracts foreign firms.
European and Japanese immigrants brought skills to São Paulo and the South.
Migrants from the Northeast came to work in the ABC factories.
Skilled engineers at São José dos Campos support aerospace, so Embraer grew there.

notes.b: Factories locate close to buyers, and Brazil has a big home market.
points: A domestic market of over 200 million people, with a growing middle class, buys cars, goods and food.
Mercosur (the trade bloc of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay) opens neighbouring markets.
Export markets take iron ore, jets, meat and other goods.

notes.h: Capital and infrastructure as location factors
notes.b: Industry needs money and links to move goods, and these are concentrated in the Southeast.
points: Coffee wealth, foreign multinationals, state firms and the BNDES development bank (1952) supplied the capital.
The port of Santos, the largest in Latin America, exports and imports for São Paulo.
The dense road network of the Southeast links factories to ports and markets.
Infrastructure is weak elsewhere, which keeps industry away from many regions.
notes.tip: The capital is Brasília, not Rio or São Paulo. São Paulo is the largest and richest city.

notes.h: Government policy as a location factor
notes.b: The state has steered where factories are built, using tariffs and incentives.
points: ISI tariffs protected home industry under Vargas and Kubitschek.
The Manaus Free Trade Zone (1967) used tax breaks to bring firms to assemble electronics, televisions, phones and motorbikes (Honda) in the Amazon.
SUDENE (Superintendency for the Development of the Northeast, 1959), led by economist Celso Furtado, gave incentives to the poorer Northeast, for example the Camaçari petrochemical complex in Bahia.
SUDAM (the Amazon development agency, 1966) did the same for the North.

notes.b: Industry is not spread evenly. It is packed into a core and thin elsewhere.
points: Industry is concentrated in the Southeast 'industrial triangle' of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte, and São Paulo state alone produces the largest share.
The concentration builds on itself (cumulative causation): factories draw workers, suppliers and services, which attract more factories, so a core region grows.
Secondary clusters are in the South (Porto Alegre, Curitiba, Joinville), in Manaus and on the Northeast coast.
notes.tip: For a question on distribution, explain the core in terms of raw materials, ports, markets and cumulative causation.

notes.b: Examiners reward named firms and places. Learn one for each industry.
points: Cars: the ABC region and Fiat (now Stellantis) at Betim, Minas Gerais.
Aircraft: Embraer at São José dos Campos.
Steel: CSN at Volta Redonda.
Oil and petrochemicals: Petrobras.
Meat processing: JBS, and pulp and paper.
Shoes and textiles: the shoe industry of the Vale dos Sinos in Rio Grande do Sul, in the South.

notes.b: Brazilian industry has struggled in recent decades.
points: The 'Brazil cost' (Custo Brasil) is the extra cost from high taxes, complex bureaucracy and poor transport.
Deindustrialisation since the 2010s means industry's share of the economy has shrunk, with competition from China.
Ford ended car production in Brazil in 2021.
Regional imbalance remains, with industry concentrated in the Southeast.

notes.b: Services are now the biggest part of the economy, and São Paulo leads them.
points: Services produce well over half of GDP and employ about seven in ten workers (early 2020s).
São Paulo is Latin America's leading financial centre, with the B3 (Brasil Bolsa Balcão) stock exchange and Avenida Paulista, its financial street.

notes.b: Rio is Brazil's best-known tourist city. Exams ask for two named attractions, so know these.
points: Christ the Redeemer, a statue on Corcovado completed in 1931, was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World (2007).
Sugarloaf Mountain (Pão de Açúcar), a granite-gneiss dome about 396 m high, and the beaches of Copacabana and Ipanema draw visitors.
Rio's landscapes between mountain and sea are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012).
Carnival parades take place in the Sambadrome, designed by Oscar Niemeyer (1984).
notes.tip: Carnival is the festival before Lent (the Catholic calendar), not a harvest festival.

notes.h: Tourist attractions: nature, culture and history
notes.b: Away from Rio, Brazil's wildlife, heritage and landscapes draw visitors.
points: Iguaçu Falls on the Brazil-Argentina border, about 275 separate falls, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Amazon offers Manaus, jungle lodges and the Teatro Amazonas, the opera house (1896) built with rubber wealth.
The Pantanal is known for wildlife, including jaguars.
Salvador's Pelourinho (the historic centre, a UNESCO site) shows Afro-Brazilian culture, and Ouro Preto is a colonial UNESCO site.
Brasília's modernist architecture is a UNESCO site (1987).
Fernando de Noronha is a marine park, and the Lençóis Maranhenses has white sand dunes with rain-filled lagoons.

notes.b: Several attractions at once make Brazil a magnet.
points: Tropical beaches and warm climate suit holidays.
Carnival and festivals bring crowds.
Unique wildlife and landscapes, such as the Amazon, Pantanal and Iguaçu Falls, draw nature lovers.
Culture, including music, football, food and Afro-Brazilian heritage, appeals to visitors.
Events such as the 2014 FIFA World Cup and the 2016 Olympics in Rio (the first in South America) put Brazil on world screens.
notes.tip: For two named attractions and why tourists come, give the attraction, what it is and what draws visitors.

notes.b: Brazil gets fewer foreign tourists than its size suggests, but home tourism is large.
points: About 6 million foreign tourists arrived in 2019, small for a country of its size, and Argentina is the largest source country.
Domestic tourism is far larger.
Long-haul distance and flight costs hold back arrivals.
Embratur, the tourism promotion agency, markets Brazil abroad.
The mega-events brought airport and metro investment in Rio.

notes.b: Tourism gives income and jobs, and can pay for protecting places.
points: Jobs and income arise in hotels, guiding, transport and restaurants.
Foreign exchange comes from visitors paying in foreign currency.
Infrastructure improves, such as the airports and metro built for the mega-events in Rio.
Eco-tourism in the Amazon and the Pantanal funds conservation, since the wildlife is the attraction.
Pride in culture grows when visitors value Carnival, music and heritage.

notes.h: Negative impacts and challenges of tourism
notes.b: Tourism also brings pollution, pressure on places and waste.
points: Crime and safety fears put visitors off.
Pollution: Guanabara Bay was polluted by sewage, an issue before the 2016 Olympic sailing events.
Fragile places suffer pressure, so Fernando de Noronha limits visitor numbers and charges an environmental fee.
Costly stadiums were left little used after the World Cup, such as the Arena da Amazônia in Manaus.
Vila Autódromo, a community, was largely evicted for the Olympic Park.
Seasonality means demand peaks around Carnival and then falls.
notes.tip: Pair each negative impact with a named place, such as Guanabara Bay or Vila Autódromo.

notes.b: Roads carry most of Brazil's freight and have opened the interior.
points: Roads carry about three-fifths of Brazil's freight (2020s).
The BR-116 runs along the eastern side of the country.
The Trans-Amazonian Highway (BR-230), about 4,000 km, opened in 1972, and long stretches are still unpaved.
The BR-163 links Cuiabá (Mato Grosso) to Santarém (Pará) on the Amazon and is the soya route, paved along most of its length by about 2020.
Roads open the Amazon to settlement and clearance. Rondônia, along the BR-364, shows the fishbone pattern of clearings along roads.
notes.tip: Keep deforestation brief: roads open the forest to settlers, so clearings spread out along them.

notes.b: Rail is small, but rivers and ports are vital for freight.
points: The rail network is small and mostly used for ore, such as the Carajás Railway to São Luís.
The Amazon and its tributaries are waterways, and the Tietê-Paraná waterway links the south.
Ports include Santos (São Paulo state), Paranaguá (Paraná), São Luís (Maranhão) and Santarém (Pará).
The 'Northern Arc' (Arco Norte) of Amazon river ports now ships much of the soya harvest.

notes.b: Distance makes air travel essential, and cities have tried new ways to move people.
points: Great distances make air travel vital, and São Paulo-Guarulhos is the busiest airport in South America.
Curitiba's bus rapid transit (BRT), begun in 1974 under mayor Jaime Lerner, has been copied worldwide.
São Paulo's metro and congestion are managed by the rodízio scheme (1997), which bans cars from the centre at rush hours on one weekday according to the last digit of the number plate.

notes.b: Transport holds a continental country together and lowers costs.
points: It integrates a country of 8.5 million km², linking regions.
It lowers export costs for soya and ore.
It opens the interior, such as Brasília and the Centre-West.
Road-building in the Amazon brings deforestation, so there is a cost.
notes.tip: For a Higher question on development of transport, give types, named routes and then importance and problems.

keyTerms.definition: The Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation, founded in 1973, which bred tropical crops and made the Cerrado productive.
The second crop of maize planted after the soya harvest in the same rainy season.
The Landless Rural Workers' Movement, founded 1984, which presses for land redistribution.
A policy of making goods at home that were once imported, protecting new factories with tariffs.
The 'Brazil cost': extra business costs from high taxes, bureaucracy and poor transport.
Oil fields discovered in 2006 to 2007 deep under the ocean floor beneath a thick layer of salt.
An area, such as Manaus (1967), where firms get tax breaks to attract industry.
A protected forest area where local people harvest products such as rubber without clearing it.
A dam that stores the waste mud from a mine.
The 1975 National Alcohol Programme to make ethanol fuel from sugar cane.

factCards.definition: Liming and fertiliser, EMBRAPA's tropical soya varieties, cheap flat land for machines and reliable summer rain.

A rubber tapper and union leader murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988. The Extractive Reserve was created in 1990.
The world's largest iron-ore mine, in Pará, run by Vale, with the ore carried about 890 km by railway to São Luís.

The warm Brazil Current is low in plankton, so there is little fish food along the coast.
Discovered in 2006 to 2007 in the Santos Basin, up to about 300 km offshore, beneath a thick layer of salt, and now supplying most of Brazil's oil.
Vargas used tariffs and built the CSN steelworks at Volta Redonda (1946); Kubitschek brought foreign car makers to the ABC region.
Set up in 1967 with tax breaks to attract assembly of electronics, phones and motorbikes in the Amazon.
São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte in the Southeast.
Ford ended car production in Brazil in 2021, a sign of deindustrialisation and the Brazil cost.
Positive: jobs, foreign exchange, infrastructure and conservation funding. Negative: pollution at Guanabara Bay, unused stadiums and evictions at Vila Autódromo.
About 4,000 km, begun in 1970 and opened in 1972, with long stretches still unpaved.

questions.prompt: Examine how two factors have influenced the development of secondary economic activity in Brazil.
questions.model: Raw materials and energy. Brazil's industry grew where its raw materials were. Iron ore from Minas Gerais and Carajás feeds steel, and the CSN steelworks at Volta Redonda began production in 1946. Carajás in Pará is the world's largest iron-ore mine, and its ore goes by railway to São Luís for export. Sugar cane is turned into ethanol, so cane in São Paulo state supports a fuel industry. Soya and meat supply food processing, such as JBS. Hydroelectricity from Itaipu, on the Paraná and shared with Paraguay, supplies the Southeast industrial core with cheap power. Tucuruí, on the Tocantins, powers aluminium smelting in the Amazon. Together these resources explain why industry clusters in the Southeast. Government policy. From the 1930s Getúlio Vargas used import substitution industrialisation, protecting factories with tariffs and building heavy industry such as the CSN steelworks and Petrobras. Under Juscelino Kubitschek (1956 to 1961) foreign car makers were invited into the ABC region near São Paulo, and Volkswagen's São Bernardo plant opened in 1959. The Manaus Free Trade Zone (1967) used tax breaks to bring electronics and motorbike assembly to the Amazon. SUDENE (1959) gave incentives to the Northeast, leading to the Camaçari petrochemical complex in Bahia. The Real Plan (1994) ended hyperinflation, and privatisation of Embraer in 1994 and Vale in 1997 opened the economy. The effect was a concentrated industrial triangle of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte, with smaller clusters at Manaus and in the Northeast.
